chapterName: Late Republic: Cicero, Catiline and the Triumvirate (63-53 BCE)

briefing.title: Rome, 63 BC
paragraphs: Rome in 63 BC rules a vast republic run by elected magistrates and a proud Senate. This year's consul is Cicero, a brilliant lawyer from outside the old nobility. His enemy Catiline, an aristocrat rejected by the voters again and again, is plotting to seize power by force.

Behind them stand three ambitious men: Pompey, Rome's greatest general; Crassus, one of its richest men; and Caesar, a rising politician. Within a decade their secret alliance will bend the republic to their will, until disaster strikes far to the east at Carrhae.

timelines.name: The Big Picture
timelines.blurb: Four turning points from Catiline's plot to civil war.

events.label: Cicero exposes Catiline's conspiracy
events.fact: As consul, Cicero denounced Catiline to his face in the Senate, and five captured plotters were later executed without trial.

events.label: Caesar's stormy consulship
events.fact: Backed by Pompey and Crassus, Caesar forced through a land law after a mob threw his fellow consul off the speakers' platform.

events.label: Crassus crushed by the Parthians
events.fact: Near Carrhae, Parthian mounted archers shattered Crassus's army; about 20,000 Romans died and Crassus was killed at truce talks.

events.label: Pompey and Caesar go to civil war
events.fact: With Crassus dead, trust between Pompey and Caesar collapsed and their rivalry exploded into civil war.

timelines.name: Plotters and Partners
timelines.blurb: From Catiline's trials to the second consulship of Pompey and Crassus.

events.label: Catiline prosecuted and acquitted
events.fact: When Catiline was prosecuted in 65 and 64 BC, former consuls spoke in his defence and he was acquitted.

events.label: Catiline dies fighting at Pistoria
events.fact: Catiline's remaining force of at least 3,000 men was destroyed near Pistoria, modern Pistoia in Tuscany.

events.label: Cicero flees into exile in Greece
events.fact: A rabble-rousing tribune passed a law banishing anyone who had executed a citizen without trial.

events.label: The allies meet at Luca
events.fact: Caesar met Pompey at Luca, modern Lucca, and some two hundred senators flocked there to curry favour.

events.label: Pompey and Crassus consuls again
events.fact: Elected amid force and bribery, they gave themselves five-year commands: Spain for Pompey and Syria for Crassus.

events.label: The rivalry turns into civil war
events.fact: As Pompey sought allies among Caesar's enemies, trust collapsed and civil war broke out.

timelines.name: Details and Aftermath
timelines.blurb: Eight sharper moments, from lost farms to a modern word.

events.label: Farmers lose their land in civil wars
events.fact: These dispossessed farmers later gave Catiline's plot its real muscle.

events.label: Five conspirators strangled
events.fact: Cicero announced their deaths with a single grim word, vixerunt, 'they have lived'.

events.label: Mob breaks the consul's fasces
events.fact: Caesar's fellow consul was thrown from the speakers' platform as he tried to block the land law, which then passed.

events.label: Pompey secures Cicero's recall
events.fact: Cicero came back from Greece the year after his banishment, thanks to Pompey, Rome's greatest general.

events.label: A tribune curses Crassus at the gate
events.fact: As Crassus left for his Syrian command, a tribune solemnly cursed him at the city gate.

events.label: Crassus's son killed after a breakout
events.when: 9 June 53 BC, according to a Roman poet
events.fact: Lured away from the Roman square at Carrhae, he was killed and his head was paraded on a spear.

events.label: The word 'triumvirate' first recorded
events.fact: No ancient writer called the alliance the 'First Triumvirate'; the term is first recorded in 1681.

matchSets.name: Latin Words
matchSets.blurb: Match each Latin word to its meaning.

pairs.name: Senatus consultum ultimum
pairs.match: Senate's final decree urging consuls to do whatever it took

pairs.name: Vixerunt
pairs.match: 'They have lived': Cicero's word announcing the executions

pairs.name: Pater patriae
pairs.match: 'Father of the fatherland', the title senators gave Cicero

pairs.name: Amicitia
pairs.match: “Friendship”, the usual Roman word for a political alliance

pairs.name: Fasces
pairs.match: Rods around an axe carried before a consul as a sign of authority

matchSets.name: Places and Powers
matchSets.blurb: Match each place or power to its role in the story.

pairs.name: Pistoria
pairs.match: Where Catiline's army was destroyed and he died fighting

pairs.name: Temple of Concord
pairs.match: Where the Senate debated the fate of the arrested plotters

pairs.name: Luca
pairs.match: Town where Caesar met Pompey to renew their pact in 56 BC

pairs.name: Parthian Empire
pairs.match: Power ruling Iran and Mesopotamia that Crassus chose to attack

pairs.name: Carrhae
pairs.match: Battlefield near modern Harran where Crassus was killed

cards.claim: When Catiline was prosecuted in 65 and 64 BC, former consuls defended him and he was acquitted.
cards.why: Catiline was no outsider: former consuls spoke for him and he was acquitted both times.

cards.claim: The first hard evidence of the plot came from Pompey, who handed over anonymous letters.
cards.why: It was Crassus, the richest man in Rome, who handed over the anonymous letters on 18 or 19 October 63 BC.

cards.claim: Reports said armed men were gathering in Campania, south of Rome.
cards.why: The armed men gathered in Etruria, the region north of Rome; an officer took up arms near Faesulae.

cards.claim: Envoys of the Allobroges, a Gallic tribe, revealed the scheme and served Cicero as double agents.
cards.why: A senior magistrate among the plotters tried to recruit them, but their envoys revealed the plan to Cicero.

cards.claim: In the Senate debate of 5 December, Caesar demanded the immediate execution of the prisoners.
cards.why: Caesar proposed life imprisonment or custody until trial; it was the senior senators who called for death.

cards.claim: Catiline died fighting when his army was destroyed near Pistoria in January 62 BC.
cards.why: His force of at least 3,000 men met the government army near Pistoria, and Catiline died in the battle.

cards.claim: In 58 BC Cicero fled into exile in Spain.
cards.why: Cicero fled to Greece and was recalled the following year thanks to Pompey.

cards.claim: Most scholars today think the plot was real but its danger was exaggerated.
cards.why: Two 1970s studies argued Cicero invented or provoked the affair, but most scholars reject that view.

cards.claim: Pompey, Crassus and Caesar struck their pact in secret, sometime between July 60 and January 59 BC.
cards.why: The three made a secret pact to back one another, which they simply called friendship (amicitia).

cards.claim: Caesar celebrated a grand triumph before standing for consul.
cards.why: Caesar gave up his triumph so that he could stand for the consulship.

cards.claim: As consul, Caesar cut the tax companies' debt by a third to please Crassus.
cards.why: After the land law passed, Caesar cut the tax companies' debt by a third and approved Pompey's eastern settlement.

cards.claim: Pompey married Crassus's daughter to seal the alliance.
cards.why: Pompey married Caesar's daughter to seal the bond.

cards.claim: Some two hundred senators flocked to Luca to curry favour with the allies.
cards.why: When Caesar met Pompey at Luca in 56 BC, about two hundred senators came to court them.

cards.claim: In 55 BC Crassus gave himself a five-year command in Spain.
cards.why: Crassus took Syria; Spain went to Pompey.

cards.claim: The Parthian army at Carrhae was made up mainly of heavy infantry.
cards.why: The Parthians fielded about 10,000 cavalry, including armoured horsemen and mounted archers resupplied by camels.

cards.claim: No ancient writer called the alliance the 'First Triumvirate'.
cards.why: The term is first recorded in 1681, and many modern historians now avoid it as misleading.

oddOneOut.why: Pompey, Crassus and Caesar made a secret pact to back one another. Cicero was not part of it; he complained of 'three men' holding kingly power.
Expelled senators, failed candidates and indebted veterans all joined Catiline's coalition. The tax-collecting businessmen were championed by Crassus and wanted their payments for Asia cut.
Drums, armoured horsemen and mounted archers were all on the Parthian side at Carrhae. The Gallic horsemen fought for Rome, brought by Crassus's son.

items: Took a five-year command in Spain
Cut tax firms' debt by a third
oddOneOut.why: The land law, the debt cut and approval of Pompey's settlement were Caesar's acts as consul in 59 BC. The Spanish command went to Pompey in 55 BC.

items: Senate meets in Temple of Concord
oddOneOut.why: The meeting, Caesar's proposal and the executions all happened in Rome on 5 December 63 BC. Catiline died later, near Pistoria in January 62 BC.

items: A short history of the plot
A poem on his own consulship
oddOneOut.why: Cicero wrote the speeches, the memoir and the poem himself. The short history was written about twenty years later by another Roman politician who had been abroad in 63 BC.

whoAmI.name: The Conspiracy of 63 BC
whoAmI.blurb: Plotter, prosecutor and a voice for mercy.

people.name: Catiline
clues: I came from an ancient family, but none of my ancestors had been consul for some four centuries.
When I was prosecuted in 65 and 64 BC, former consuls spoke in my defence.
After losing the elections of autumn 63 BC, I decided to seize power by force.
I died fighting when my army was destroyed near Pistoria.

people.name: Cicero
clues: I published my speeches around 60 BC and wrote a poem celebrating my own consulship.
Two volunteers agreed to murder me, but their attempt failed the next morning.
I announced the executions of five plotters with a single word: vixerunt.
As consul in 63 BC, I crushed a conspiracy and was hailed as 'father of the fatherland'.

people.name: Caesar
clues: A stern young senator hinted that I secretly sympathised with the plotters.
I was a rising politician due to take high office in the year after the plot.
In the debate of 5 December 63 BC, I proposed life imprisonment instead of death.
I later won a five-year command in Gaul and grew rich from my victories there.

whoAmI.name: The Three Allies
whoAmI.blurb: The men behind the so-called 'First Triumvirate'.

people.name: Pompey
clues: I married my ally's daughter to seal our bond.
I said that if anyone raised a sword against the land law, I would bring a shield.
I came back from a long war against the king of Pontus wanting land for my veterans.
As consul in 55 BC, I gave myself a five-year command in Spain.

people.name: Crassus
clues: I grew rich buying up confiscated property during the civil wars.
A tribune solemnly cursed me at the city gate as I left Rome in November 55 BC.
I twice refused the Armenian king's offer of a safer route through Armenia.
After my army was defeated at Carrhae, I was killed during truce talks.

people.name: Caesar
clues: In 56 BC I met one ally at Ravenna and the other at Luca.
I had a conservative senator dragged off to jail for talking endlessly against my land law.
I gave up a triumph so that I could stand for consul.
As consul in 59 BC I passed a land law, then received a five-year command in Gaul.

places.name: Pistoria
places.why: Near Pistoria, modern Pistoia in Tuscany, Catiline's army was destroyed and he died fighting in January 62 BC.

places.name: Carrhae
places.why: Near Carrhae, modern Harran, Parthian cavalry destroyed Crassus's army in 53 BC.

places.name: Syria
places.why: Crassus took Syria as his five-year command and wintered there before invading Mesopotamia.

places.name: Gaul
places.why: Caesar's command in Gaul brought him conquests, honours and wealth that made him no longer a junior partner.

places.name: Spain
places.why: Caesar returned from governing southern Spain in 60 BC, and in 55 BC Pompey took Spain as his five-year command.

places.name: Mesopotamia
places.why: Crassus marched into Mesopotamia, part of the Parthian Empire, in spring 53 BC to win military glory.
